title: Incremental Processing in the Age of Non-Incremental Encoders: An Empirical Assessment of Bidirectional Models for Incremental NLU
text:
In “The Story of Your Life”, a science fiction short story by Ted [1], Earth is visited by alien creatures whose writing system does not unfold in time but rather presents full thoughts instantaneously. In our world, however, language does unfold over time, both in speaking and in writing. There is ample evidence [2,3] that it is also processed over time by humans, in an incremental fashion where the interpretation of a full utterance is continuously built up while the utterance is being perceived.

In Computational Linguistics and Natural Language Processing, this property is typically abstracted away by assuming that the unit to be processed (e.g., a sentence) is available as a whole. The return and subsequent mainstreaming of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), originally introduced by [9] and repopularized i.a. by [10], may have made it seem that time had found a place as a first-class citizen in NLP. However, it was quickly discovered that certain technical issues of this type of model could be overcome, for example in the application of machine translation, by encoding input sequences in reverse temporal order [11].

This turns out to be a special case of the more general strategy of bidirectional processing, proposed earlier in the form of BiRNNs [12,13] and BiLSTMs [14], which combine a forward and a backward pass over a sequence. More recently, Transformers [15] also function with representations that inherently have no notion of linear order. Atemporal processing has thus become the standard again.

In this paper, we explore whether we can adapt such bidirectional models to work in incremental processing mode and what the performance cost is of doing so. We first go back and reproduce the work of [16], who compare the performance of LSTMs and BiLSTMs in sequence tagging, extending it with a BERT-based encoder and with a collection of different datasets for tagging and classification tasks. Then we address the following questions:

Q1. If we employ inherently non-incremental models in an incremental system, do we get functional representations that are adequate to build correct and stable output along the way? We examine how bidirectional encoders behave under an incremental interface, revisiting the approach proposed by [17] for POS taggers. After standard training, we modify the testing procedure by allowing the system to see only successively extended prefixes of the input available so far with which they must produce successively extended prefixes of the output, as shown in Figure 1. The evaluation metrics are described in Section 3, and the discussion is anchored on the concepts of timeliness, monotonicity, and decisiveness and their trade-off with respect to the non-incremental quality [17,18]. We show that it is possible to use them as components of an incremental system (e.g. for NLU) with some trade-offs.

Q2. How can we adapt the training regime or the real-time procedure to mitigate the negative effect that the non-availability of right context (i.e., future parts of the signal) has on non-incremental models? To tackle this question, we implement three strategies that help improve the models’ incremental quality: truncated training, delayed output and prophecies (see Section 4).

Our results are relevant for incremental Natural Language Understanding, needed for the design of dialogue systems and more generally interactive systems, e.g. those following the incremental processing model proposed by [19]. These systems rely on the availability of partial results, on which fast decisions can be based. Similarly, simultaneous translation is an area where decisions need to be based on partial input with incomplete syntactical and semantic information.
